children: By Maya Davis

WASHINGTON-House lawmakers are heading home until after the elections, getting an early dismissal despite simmering concerns about high gasoline prices and the dangers of artificial intelligence-and criticism that Congress just isn't doing its job.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R., La.) insisted that letting lawmakers go this week-rather than later this month-is the best path for GOP candidates in the final campaign stretch until November's general election. Leaders had already called off two weeks of scheduled work this month, and on Wednesday said that was the last day, cutting planned votes Thursday.

"Congress is not on recess," Johnson told reporters Tuesday. "Our members can be doing more and better work for their constituents and their districts over the next couple weeks than here, just kind of running in circles."

Johnson said Wednesday, by his count, that the House has had its second most productive session since 1789, boasting of more than 900 bills passed while blaming the Senate for not getting them over the finish line. As of last week, 104 laws have been enacted in the current Congress, putting it on pace for fewer than any of its predecessors since the Civil War.

Earlier this month, Congress cleared a crucial short-term funding law, putting a possible shutdown past the election. But House GOP lawmakers say the Senate, also led by Republicans, has held up major proposals including the SAVE America Act, a key Trump priority that would impose stricter voting rules. Johnson said if the Senate moved on legislation, he would bring his chamber "back with a 48 hours' notice, and we'll stay here indefinitely."
A Senate GOP aide called the criticism of the Senate laughable and said the House was leaving town early to avoid making members take hard votes.

Johnson dismissed speculation that he had sent lawmakers home early to put off a vote forced by Iran war critic Rep. Thomas Massie (R., Ky.) on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. And Johnson said that while some members were clamoring for a vote on suspending the gas tax, there was no consensus yet. Both parties see any artificial-intelligence legislation as a ways off, with Sen. John Kennedy (R., La.) airing his frustrations over the slow pace of progress.
"Right now, Congress can't pass gas," he said.

Congress has been struggling with low marks from Americans for decades, but repeated government shutdowns, standoffs and intraparty squabbles of late have taken a further toll. President Trump's moves to wrench power from Congress on war, tariffs and spending have also hit the institution's reputation. An April Gallup poll put congressional disapproval at 86%, a historic high.
Asked why this Congress's approval ratings are among the weakest, Rep. Tim Burchett (R., Tenn.) said it is because of "the truth."
"I've been here eight years, and like I say, these post offices aren't gonna name themselves," Burchett joked. He conceded he would have liked to see several of his bills move.

Congress is known for short workweeks in D.C. and long breaks so members can spend time in their home states. Congressional leaders put out a calendar of what days lawmakers should expect to be in Washington for votes, which was more than 100 days this year. But cancellations like those this month whittle that total number down, as did a long break last year during the government shutdown.

"Canceling yet another day of votes is unacceptable," Rep. Ralph Norman (R., S.C.) posted to X on Wednesday, putting the number of canceled voting days at 63 since this Congress started in January 2025. "The Founders did not envision taking this much time off and still getting paid."
Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle said the House has unfinished business and they wanted to stick around.
"If I were speaker for a day, I would not recess us until our work was done, and our work is far from done," said Rep. Kat Cammack (R., Fla.). She said AI concerns still need to be addressed.
Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D., Wash.) said the House shouldn't be leaving early, but she would rather be in her district because the chamber doesn't "do anything of value here."
"If they were running a responsible Congress, no, they should not be continuing to cancel sessions," she added.

The Democratic and Republican women's caucuses introduced a bipartisan measure to combat sexual misconduct in May, which DWC chair Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D., N.M.) said would be held up because of the early recess, during a time when the House Ethics Committee is investigating multiple members for sexual misconduct.
"We have bipartisan support for it, but when you cancel legislative days, it shrinks our ability to get that work done," she said.

The House is falling behind the Senate on hours and voting days this Congress, according to an analysis by the centrist group No Labels. From Jan. 1 to Aug. 31, the Senate has spent 667 hours in session against the House's 383. The Senate is scheduled to be in session until later this month, though there has been speculation that it might get cut short as well.
Despite Congress's increasingly poor reputation, some experts say this year's work hasn't been an anomaly.

"How you measure productivity is truly all over the place," said J.D. Rackey, associate director of the Structural Democracy Project at the Bipartisan Policy Center. "Some of the metrics, the current Congress is kind of within the average of all the Congresses. That's not an outlier by any means."
